title: One and Zero: the Court Librarian, the Calculus, and the Letter from Beijing
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Leipzig, the birth at the Nikolaikirche
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day; born 1 July 1646, baptized at the Nikolaikirche
stops.campa: On the first of July a son is born in Leipzig to Friedrich Leibniz, professor of moral philosophy, and carried to the Nikolaikirche to be baptized. The father dies when the boy is six and leaves behind a private library which the household lets him enter unsupervised. He teaches himself Latin there before he is twelve, reading the Roman historians and the scholastics in whatever order the shelves happen to present them. No tutor sets the sequence and no examiner checks the result. He is being educated by a dead man's furniture.
suggested_refs: The Nikolaikirche, Leipzig, parish church of the Leibniz family
Friedrich Leibniz's private library, dispersed after 1652
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: University of Leipzig, matriculation at fourteen
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month and day unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: At fourteen he matriculates at the university where his father taught, taken up by Jakob Thomasius, who had himself studied under Friedrich Leibniz. Bachelor of philosophy in 1662, master in 1664, bachelor of law in 1665. The curriculum is Aristotle and the scholastics. On his own hours he reads Bacon and Galileo and the mechanical philosophy the faculty does not teach, and he is already trying to reconcile the two bodies of thought rather than choose between them. His 1663 disputation on the principle of individuation is the first surviving attempt.
suggested_refs: Leibniz's 1663 bachelor's disputation, Disputatio Metaphysica de Principio Individui
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Jena, a summer with Erhard Weigel
stops.date_confidence: attested to the summer term of 1663; the day is a convention
stops.campa: He spends a term at the Collegium Jenense with the mathematician Erhard Weigel, who holds that philosophical demonstration should be conducted on the model of mathematical proof: definitions laid down, consequences drawn, disagreements ended by inspection rather than by shouting. Leibniz is seventeen and stays a single term before returning to Leipzig. He works at that proposition for the next fifty years, in the calculus of reasoning and in the machine that computes for you, and never finishes the demonstration language it would need.
suggested_refs: Erhard Weigel's mathematical teaching at Jena and its influence on the characteristica universalis
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Leipzig, De Arte Combinatoria and the doctorate refused
stops.date_confidence: year attested for both the habilitation and the refusal; the order within the year is not fixed
stops.campa: At nineteen he defends the habilitation thesis that becomes his first book, De Arte Combinatoria, a treatise on the recombination of simple concepts which already sketches a general calculus of reasoning. The same year the law faculty declines to give him his doctorate. His youth is the reason offered; other accounts speak of a dean's grudge. He makes no public quarrel of it and leaves for Altdorf within the year. Which of the two reasons was the real one, the record does not say.
stops.quote: a language or characteristic which includes at once both the arts of discovery and judgement, that is, one whose signs and characters serve the same purpose that arithmetical signs serve for numbers
stops.quote_source: Leibniz on the characteristica universalis, quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Characteristica universalis'
suggested_refs: De Arte Combinatoria (Leipzig, 1666), Leibniz's first book
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Altdorf, the doctorate and the chair declined
stops.date_confidence: sources differ and are not reconciled here: German Wikipedia gives November 1666, MacTutor February 1667, SEP simply 1667
stops.campa: Altdorf examines him within months and awards the doctorate in law for a thesis on perplexing cases, De Casibus Perplexis, then offers him a professorship on the spot. He turns it down. His thoughts, he says, are turned in an entirely different direction. At twenty he has closed the academic career that Leipzig would not open for him and holds no employment of any kind, no patron, and no income beyond what his family can spare. The sources put the doctorate variously in November 1666 and February 1667. He rides on to Nuremberg.
suggested_refs: De Casibus Perplexis in Jure (Altdorf, 1666), the doctoral thesis
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Nuremberg, secretary to the alchemists
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: His first salaried post is secretary to a Nuremberg society devoted to alchemy, a subject about which he knows almost nothing on the day he applies. He keeps its minutes and copies its recipes, learning the vocabulary of transmutation from inside the room at an age when his contemporaries are clerking in provincial courts. He enters the discipline through its notation long before he believes a word of its claims, which is how he enters every discipline afterwards. The society's meeting house is not recorded. Its membership roll has not survived.
suggested_refs: The Nuremberg alchemical society of the 1660s, meeting place unrecorded
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Frankfurt, the Römerberg, meeting Boineburg
stops.date_confidence: attested as by November 1667; the exact day is not recorded
stops.campa: At Frankfurt he meets Johann Christian von Boineburg, lately dismissed as chief minister to the Elector of Mainz and still one of the best connected men in Germany. Boineburg takes him into private service as librarian, legal draftsman and writer of letters. Through him Leibniz enters the world of courts, embassies and confessional diplomacy, and begins the correspondence that will run to hundreds of names in a dozen countries. The daily work is cataloguing another man's books and drafting another man's letters, and he does it for five years.
suggested_refs: Boineburg's library and papers, Leibniz's first charge in court service
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Mainz, the legal code and the Egyptian plan
stops.date_confidence: the appointment runs 1669-1672; the research pool's chronology lens dated it 1667 and contradicted its own geography lens, which is followed here
stops.campa: Boineburg's patronage carries him into the Elector's own service. He is named assessor to the Court of Appeal and set to reforming the electorate's legal code, and in these years he writes the Catholic Demonstrations, an attempt to argue the Roman and Lutheran churches back into a single body. Between drafts he works on the characteristica universalis, a script in which every concept would have its sign and every dispute could be settled by computation instead of by war. He also gives the project a schedule.
stops.quote: I think that some selected men could finish the matter in five years.
stops.quote_source: Leibniz on the characteristica universalis, quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Characteristica universalis'
suggested_refs: The Kurfürstliches Schloss at Mainz
The Catholic Demonstrations, begun c. 1668-1669
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Paris, arrival on a mission nobody wants
stops.date_confidence: arrival attested to October 1672; the day is not recorded, and no Paris address survives for any of the four years
stops.campa: He arrives in Paris carrying a memorandum for Louis XIV: that France should conquer Egypt rather than invade the Rhineland, seizing the road to the Indies and leaving the German princes alone. It is a diversion dressed as strategy, and the French court never grants him the audience to present it. Boineburg dies that December and the Elector of Mainz the following February, which ends the errand altogether. He stays four years anyway, without a post and without a salary. No Paris address survives for any of them.
suggested_refs: The Egypt memorandum drafted for Boineburg, addressed to Louis XIV
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: London, Arundel House, the Stepped Reckoner
stops.date_confidence: visit attested to January-February 1673; venue corrected from Gresham College, which the Royal Society reoccupied only later in 1673, to Arundel House on the Strand
stops.campa: Sent to London as escort on a peace errand, he brings the calculating machine he has been building since 1670, a stepped drum mechanism that multiplies and divides rather than merely adding. He demonstrates it to the Royal Society at Arundel House, where the Society still meets while Gresham College is repaired after the Fire, and is elected a Fellow on the ninth of April. He also meets Henry Oldenburg and John Collins. Both introductions will be read against him forty years later, by men holding his own letters.
stops.quote: We know that respectable and modest people prefer it when they think of something that is consistent with what someone else discovered, to ascribe their own improvements and additions to the discoverer, so as not to arouse suspicions of intellectual dishonesty; the desire for true generosity should pursue them, instead of the lying thirst for dishonest profit.
stops.quote_source: Leibniz, letter to Henry Oldenburg, 1673, quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Leibniz-Newton calculus controversy'
suggested_refs: The Stepped Reckoner, Leibniz's calculating machine, begun 1670
Arundel House on the Strand, temporary home of the Royal Society 1666-1673
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Paris, in Christiaan Huygens's hands
stops.date_confidence: the tutelage runs across 1672-1676; this stop fixes it to mid-1673 as a convention
stops.campa: Christiaan Huygens takes the self-taught lawyer in hand and sets him to read Pascal and Descartes, whose measure of force Leibniz will spend the rest of his life attacking. The mathematics he thought he understood turns out to be a decade behind the front. He works through it in private notebooks, and by 1675 holds a differential and integral calculus arrived at independently of Newton's earlier, unpublished fluxions. Ehrenfried Walther von Tschirnhaus reaches Paris that year and becomes his friend. None of it is printed for another nine years.
suggested_refs: Huygens's Paris circle, 1672-1676
Pascal's unpublished mathematical manuscripts, read by Leibniz in Paris
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Paris, the Academy has no vacancy
stops.date_confidence: year attested; venue is the King's Library, where the Academy sat before the 1699 move to the Louvre
stops.campa: He applies to the Académie Royale des Sciences as a foreign honorary member and is refused for want of a vacancy. The Academy sits at this date in the King's Library, not yet in the Louvre rooms it will occupy after the reorganization of 1699. He is at this moment writing the calculus into his notebooks and cannot obtain a salaried place in the city where he is writing it. Admission comes around 1700, when his reputation no longer requires it; the sources give 1700 and 1701 and do not agree.
suggested_refs: The Académie Royale des Sciences in the King's Library, before its 1699 installation at the Louvre
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Paris, the twenty-ninth of October
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day from the dated manuscript page
stops.campa: On a single sheet dated the twenty-ninth of October he writes down the long S for a sum of infinitesimals, and shortly afterwards the letter d for a difference. The signs are chosen for the operations they make easy to write rather than for any metaphysics behind them, and they survive on exactly that ground. Newton's dotted fluxions, worked out earlier, fall out of use within a century. The sheet is a working page in a private notebook, and he prints nothing from it until 1684.
suggested_refs: The manuscript page of 29 October 1675, first use of the integral sign
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: London, the papers of John Collins
stops.date_confidence: attested to October 1676; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: Passing through London on the road from Paris to Hanover, he calls on John Collins and is shown manuscripts of Isaac Newton's work on infinite series. This week becomes the central charge of the priority dispute: Newton will later date the theft to it, and the Royal Society will build a dossier around it. Leibniz has been writing his own calculus into his notebooks for a year already, and says so, and is not believed in London. How long he held the papers, how much he copied and what he understood are settled by no surviving document.
suggested_refs: John Collins's collection of Newton manuscripts on infinite series
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Delft, the lenses of Antoni van Leeuwenhoek
stops.date_confidence: attested to November 1676; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: He breaks the journey at Delft to see Antoni van Leeuwenhoek's microscopes, the ground lenses that have just opened the world of animalcules to European science. Leibniz folds what he sees straight into his metaphysics: a universe with no gap anywhere in it, matter divisible without end, every drop of water a pond full of living things and every one of those a world again. He is travelling with his household goods, between a city that would not employ him and a court that will. He does not record what was on the slide.
suggested_refs: Van Leeuwenhoek's single-lens microscopes at Delft

stops.name: The Hague, four days on the Paviljoensgracht
stops.date_confidence: attested to 18-21 November 1676 by SEP; coordinates corrected to the Spinozahuis at Paviljoensgracht 72-74
stops.campa: For four days in November he sits with Baruch Spinoza and goes through the Ethics, finished and unpublished, in conversation. Spinoza dies on the twenty-first of February following. For the remaining forty years of his own life Leibniz will separate his system from Spinoza's in print, at length and repeatedly, because a Lutheran courtier cannot afford the association. His private papers show a reader who had gone through the man line by line. What was said across the table those four days is recorded only in Leibniz's own notes.
suggested_refs: The Spinozahuis, Paviljoensgracht 72-74, The Hague
Spinoza's Ethics, unpublished at the date of the visit
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Hanover, the Leineschloss
stops.date_confidence: arrival attested to December 1676; coordinates corrected to the Leineschloss proper
stops.campa: He arrives in December to take up the post of counsellor to the Duke of Brunswick-Lüneburg, an offer he accepted the previous year without enthusiasm and then delayed answering for months. He will serve three successive rulers of this house for forty years, cataloguing, advising, drafting, arguing dynastic claims, and spending much of that time trying to be sent somewhere else. Within a year he is librarian of the ducal library and Privy Counselor of Justice. He holds the second title until the day he dies.
suggested_refs: The Leineschloss, Hanover, seat of the Brunswick-Lüneburg court
The ducal library at Hanover, later the Leibniz-Bibliothek
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Herrenhausen, the walks with Electress Sophia
stops.date_confidence: the friendship runs from the 1680s to Sophia's death in 1714; this stop fixes a beginning by convention
stops.campa: In the formal walks of the Herrenhausen gardens he talks philosophy for hours with the Electress Sophia, granddaughter of James the First of England and one of the very few people at this court who takes his ideas seriously rather than merely tolerating them. The conversation runs for more than thirty years and continues by letter whenever either is away. Her daughter Sophie Charlotte becomes his pupil and will later push his academy through the Berlin court. The letters are in the Hanover archive; what was said in the garden is not.
suggested_refs: The Great Garden at Herrenhausen
The Leibniz-Sophia correspondence, Hanover archive

stops.name: Clausthal-Zellerfeld, windmills over the silver
stops.date_confidence: the Harz project runs 1680-1685; the day is a convention
stops.campa: He proposes to drain the Harz silver mines with windmill-driven pumps, arguing that wind can supplement the streams that fail every winter, and spends long stretches away from Hanover overseeing trials in the shafts and on the ridges above them. Out of the same years come his first sustained thoughts on the conservation of force, and the fossil beds in the Harz strata that will feed the Protogaea. Meanwhile the court librarian stands in the wet dark of a mine, arguing with practical engineers about gearing.
suggested_refs: The Harz silver workings at Clausthal-Zellerfeld
Protogaea, Leibniz's geological work, drafted from Harz observations

stops.name: Leipzig, Nova Methodus in the Acta Eruditorum
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the Acta issue is October 1684
stops.campa: Nova Methodus pro Maximis et Minimis appears in the Acta Eruditorum, the Leipzig journal founded two years earlier by Otto Mencke and filled in its first years with Leibniz's articles, thirteen of them in four years. Six pages, badly proofread, and the first printed calculus in the world. It comes out in the town whose law faculty refused him a doctorate eighteen years before. The notation is on the page: d for the differential, and two years later, in De Geometria Recondita, the long S for the integral.
suggested_refs: Nova Methodus pro Maximis et Minimis, Acta Eruditorum, October 1684
De Geometria Recondita, Acta Eruditorum, 1686
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Clausthal-Zellerfeld, the pumps abandoned
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Duke Ernst August ends the Harz windmill project as a costly failure. Five years of trials, of pumps that clog and gears that shear and mining officials who resent the philosopher sent down to instruct them, close with the machinery taken apart. The same duke commissions him instead to write the history of the House of Brunswick, tracing its descent through the Este back toward Charlemagne. He accepts it in the same year the pumps come down, and works at it for the next thirty-one years.
suggested_refs: Duke Ernst August's order closing the Harz drainage works, 1685

stops.name: Hanover, the Discourse and the letters to Arnauld
stops.date_confidence: composition attested to early 1686; the day is a convention
stops.campa: He writes the Discourse on Metaphysics in a few weeks and sends a summary of its articles to Antoine Arnauld, the old adversary of the Jesuits, half expecting agreement. Arnauld replies that the doctrine is monstrous: if every predicate is already contained in the notion of its subject, then human freedom is finished and God is a bookkeeper. The correspondence that follows is the first sustained defense of the system Leibniz has been building in private for a decade. The Discourse itself stays in the drawer and is printed in 1846.
suggested_refs: The Discourse on Metaphysics (1686), first printed 1846
The Leibniz-Arnauld correspondence
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Vienna, the Hofburg, first leg of the archive road
stops.date_confidence: the journey departs Hanover November 1687 and reaches Vienna by 1688; the day is a convention
stops.campa: He leaves Hanover in November 1687 on the archival journey the Brunswick history requires and reaches Vienna, where he stays months at the imperial court, reading in the Habsburg collections and pressing the Emperor with proposals: a Danube canal, a state bank, an imperial academy of sciences. Nothing comes of any of them in his lifetime. The genealogy is real work and also a warrant, since a librarian on the road can call on courts that a librarian at home cannot. He will be away nearly three years.
suggested_refs: The imperial court at the Hofburg, Vienna, 1688
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Rome, the Collegio Romano and the librarianship declined
stops.date_confidence: the Rome stay is attested to 1689; the month is a convention
stops.campa: In Rome he works among the Jesuits of the Collegio Romano, several of them veterans of the China mission, and is elected to the Accademia Fisico-Matematica. An old curiosity about Chinese thought turns here into working correspondence with men who have lived at the Kangxi court and read the classics in the original. He is also sounded out for the post of Vatican Librarian, an extraordinary offer to a Lutheran. It comes to nothing, because he will not convert and does not pretend otherwise. The Este documents are still four hundred miles north.
suggested_refs: The Collegio Romano and its China-mission Jesuits
The Accademia Fisico-Matematica, Rome
sources: Perkins, Leibniz and China: A Commerce of Light (2004)

stops.name: Florence, the Medici archives
stops.date_confidence: the Florence stay falls in 1689; the month is a convention
stops.campa: In Florence he works through the Medici collections and the Laurenziana, hunting charters that might tie the Guelf house of Brunswick to the Italian Este. He meets Vincenzo Viviani, Galileo's last pupil, and sees at close range the instruments of a science one generation older than his own. The thread he is following is thin and medieval, and the stake is precedence: if the descent holds, Hanover can claim rank among the German houses. He spends his days reading charters in a hand four hundred years old.
suggested_refs: The Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Florence
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Modena, the proof in the Este archives
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: In the Este archives at Modena he finds what the whole Italian journey was for: documents establishing, to his satisfaction and his duke's, that the Guelfs of Brunswick and the Este of Ferrara come of one stock. The dynastic point is settled and can be argued in any chancery in Europe. The history built around it, the Annales Imperii Occidentis Brunsvicenses, he will work at for another twenty-six years and never finish. It is printed a century after his death, from the notes.
suggested_refs: The Este archives at the Palazzo Ducale, Modena
Annales Imperii Occidentis Brunsvicenses, unfinished at Leibniz's death

stops.name: Venice, the Marciana and the road home
stops.date_confidence: the itinerary runs November 1687 to June 1690; the Venice month is a convention. The storm and rosary story is tradition, from the eulogy literature, not from a document
stops.campa: Venice is among the last stops of an itinerary that has run through Munich, Vienna, Rome, Naples, Florence, Modena and Bologna, nearly three years of post roads with a trunk of transcripts. He reads in the Marciana and then turns north for Hanover and a duke who has been waiting a very long time for a book. On the Adriatic crossing, by one account, the ship is caught in a storm and he keeps his hands off the sailors' rosary, unwilling to counterfeit a piety he does not hold. The story comes from his eulogists.
suggested_refs: The Biblioteca Marciana, Venice
Fontenelle's éloge, source of the storm anecdote
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Wolfenbüttel, the catalogue
stops.date_confidence: appointment attested to 1691, held to 1716; coordinates corrected to the Herzog August Bibliothek
stops.campa: He is appointed librarian of the Herzog August Bibliothek at Wolfenbüttel, one of the great collections of Europe, and administers it alongside the Hanover post without ever living in the town. He designs an alphabetical author catalogue and a subject catalogue meant to be used against each other, a scheme other European libraries copy. He argues, in memoranda nobody acts on, for a general inventory of everything known, on the ground that most of what is known is in nobody's book.
stops.quote: I am convinced that the unwritten knowledge scattered among men of different callings surpasses in quantity and in importance anything we find in books, and that the greater part of our wealth has yet to be recorded.
stops.quote_source: Leibniz, Discours touchant la méthode de la certitude et de l'art d'inventer (c. 1688-1690), quoted on Wikiquote
suggested_refs: The Herzog August Bibliothek, Wolfenbüttel, and Leibniz's catalogue scheme

stops.name: Paris, the New System in the Journal des Sçavans
stops.date_confidence: published June-July 1695 in Paris; the research pool placed this at Hanover, which is where it was written, not published
stops.campa: The Journal des Sçavans prints his Systeme nouveau de la nature et de la communication des substances, and twenty years of private philosophy become public in four pages. Substances do not act on one another; each unfolds its own nature from inside, and the agreement between them is a harmony established at the beginning, like clocks set once and never touched again. Objections arrive at once, Pierre Bayle's among them, and he answers every one. He is forty-eight and has published almost nothing.
suggested_refs: Système nouveau de la nature, Journal des Sçavans, June-July 1695
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Berlin, the Academy founded
stops.date_confidence: attested to 11 July 1700; coordinates corrected to the Society's early seat in the Marstall on Dorotheenstraße
stops.campa: On the eleventh of July the Brandenburg Society of Sciences is founded in Berlin with Leibniz as its first president, pushed through the court by his former pupil Sophie Charlotte. He designs it to earn its own keep, funded out of a monopoly on the printing of calendars, and to do work rather than to ornament a reign. He presides mostly by letter, from Hanover, at a distance of two hundred miles. Leonhard Euler takes the mathematics directorship of this same body forty-four years later and works throughout in Leibniz's notation.
suggested_refs: The Brandenburg Society of Sciences, founded 11 July 1700, later the Prussian Academy

stops.name: Beijing, Joachim Bouvet posts the hexagrams
stops.date_confidence: letter attested to 4 November 1701; location corrected from the Portuguese Nantang to the French mission inside the Imperial City, the site that becomes the Beitang
stops.campa: From the French Jesuit mission inside the Imperial City, Joachim Bouvet writes to Hanover on the fourth of November and encloses a diagram of the sixty-four hexagrams of the I Ching in the arrangement attributed to Fuxi and to Shao Yong. Broken and unbroken lines, six deep, running through every combination there is. The letter will take seventeen months to reach Germany. Leibniz has been working on an arithmetic of one and zero since about 1679, and has already told his own duke what he believes it demonstrates.
stops.quote: [A concept that] is not easy to impart to the pagans, is the creation ex nihilo through God's almighty power. Now one can say that nothing in the world can better present and demonstrate this power than the origin of numbers, as it is presented here through the simple and unadorned presentation of One and Zero or Nothing.
stops.quote_source: Leibniz, letter to Rudolph Augustus, Duke of Brunswick, accompanying the I Ching hexagrams (undated in source; after 1701), quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Binary number' after J. E. H. Smith 2008, p. 415
suggested_refs: Bouvet's letter of 4 November 1701 with the Fuxi hexagram diagram
The French Jesuit residence in the Imperial City, completed 1702, later the Beitang
sources: Perkins, Leibniz and China: A Commerce of Light (2004)

stops.name: Hanover, Explication de l'Arithmétique Binaire
stops.date_confidence: the diagram reaches Hanover April 1703 and the essay is composed that year; the Académie's Mémoires volume for 1703 was not printed until 1705
stops.campa: The hexagram diagram reaches him in April 1703 and he writes the Explication de l'Arithmétique Binaire, laying out a number system built from nothing but 0 and 1 and appending Bouvet's Chinese material as evidence. He does not treat the resemblance as a coincidence or a curiosity. On his reading the Chinese sages held the binary sequence three thousand years ago, their descendants lost the key to their own figures, and he has now handed it back to them. The Paris Academy prints the paper in the Mémoires volume for 1703, which appears in 1705.
stops.quote: this restitution of their meaning, after such a great interval of time, will seem all the more curious
stops.quote_source: Leibniz, Explication de l'Arithmétique Binaire (1703), quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Binary number'
suggested_refs: Explication de l'Arithmétique Binaire, Mémoires de l'Académie Royale des Sciences for 1703, printed 1705
sources: Perkins, Leibniz and China: A Commerce of Light (2004)
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: London, Fatio's charge
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Nicolas Fatio de Duillier prints an accusation in London: that Isaac Newton was the first inventor of the calculus and that Leibniz, a second inventor at best, borrowed from him. Fatio is a Genevan mathematician, close to Newton, and a Fellow of the Royal Society. Leibniz is a Fellow too, of twenty-six years' standing, elected in 1673 on the strength of a calculating machine. Nothing much follows for five years, and the accusation sits in print, in English, unwithdrawn. The Society disavows neither the charge nor the man who made it.
suggested_refs: Fatio de Duillier's 1699 tract on the invention of the calculus

stops.name: Amsterdam, the Théodicée
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: The Essais de Théodicée appear at Amsterdam, the only full-length philosophical book he publishes in his lifetime, grown largely out of conversations with Sophie Charlotte, who has died at thirty-six. God, having conceived every possible world, made real the one holding the greatest variety compatible with the greatest order; the evil in it is the price of that arrangement and no other arrangement would come out better. The book makes him famous across Europe. Half a century later Voltaire will make it a joke that outlives the argument.
suggested_refs: Essais de Théodicée sur la bonté de Dieu (Amsterdam, 1710)

stops.name: London, John Keill's reply
stops.date_confidence: corrected from the research pool's 1708 and 1710: MacTutor places the quoted phrase in Keill's 1711 reply to Leibniz's complaint, not in an earlier review. Newton's approval is asserted by the pool but not by MacTutor
stops.campa: John Keill charges in the Philosophical Transactions that Leibniz published Newton's calculus under changed names and altered notation. Leibniz complains formally to the Royal Society, as a Fellow of it, and asks for a retraction. Keill answers instead, saying Newton's letters sent through Oldenburg in the 1670s contained enough for anyone to work from. The Society's president, who must rule on the complaint, is Newton. Leibniz petitions the same body twice more, and the second petition produces a committee.
stops.quote: pretty plain indications... whence Leibniz derived the principles of that calculus or at least could have derived them
stops.quote_source: John Keill, reply to Leibniz in the Transactions of the Royal Society of London (1711), quoted in the MacTutor biography of Leibniz
suggested_refs: Keill's papers in the Philosophical Transactions, 1711
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'
Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: London, Crane Court, the Commercium Epistolicum
stops.date_confidence: committee sits 1712, report circulated from early 1713; London Royal Society pin inherited byte-identical from newton.journey.json, which carries the same event
stops.campa: At its house in Crane Court off Fleet Street the Royal Society appoints a committee to examine the calculus dispute. It sits for some seven weeks, hears nothing from Leibniz, and issues the Commercium Epistolicum, a dossier of correspondence assembled to prove Newton first and Leibniz a plagiarist. Newton chooses the documents, writes the report, and afterwards reviews it anonymously in the Society's own journal. Modern historians hold that the two men arrived at the calculus independently of each other.
stops.quote: not a single previously unsolved problem was solved
stops.quote_source: Newton on Leibniz's mathematical papers, quoted in the MacTutor biography of Leibniz; the exact original wording is not verified against the Commercium Epistolicum itself
suggested_refs: Commercium Epistolicum (Royal Society, 1712)
Crane Court, Fleet Street, home of the Royal Society from 1710
sources: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'

stops.name: Basel, Johann Bernoulli takes up the pen
stops.date_confidence: year attested; month unrecorded, defaulted to 01-01
stops.campa: Johann Bernoulli, who has used the differential calculus longer and better than anyone in Europe outside Hanover, enters the quarrel on Leibniz's side from Basel, publishing anonymously and going after Newton's mathematics first and his character afterwards. Leibniz circulates the letters. The dispute is no longer about who wrote what first. The continental mathematicians work in d and the long S; the English keep the fluxions, and keep them alone, for most of the next century.
suggested_refs: Bernoulli's anonymous interventions in the priority dispute, 1713

stops.name: Vienna, Imperial Court Councillor
stops.date_confidence: the Vienna residence runs from late 1712 to September 1714; the day is a convention
stops.campa: He goes to Vienna on court business and stays two years, appointed Imperial Court Councillor to Charles the Sixth and pressing again, as he pressed in 1688, for an imperial academy of sciences. He is sixty-six and out of favor at home. In Vienna he is within reach of the Habsburg archives and of Prince Eugene of Savoy, who is said to have asked him plainly what his philosophy amounted to. That Prince Eugene prompted the writing which follows is tradition, repeated everywhere and documented in nothing reachable.
suggested_refs: The Habsburg court at Vienna, 1712-1714
Leibniz's proposals for an imperial academy of sciences

stops.name: Vienna, the ninety paragraphs
stops.date_confidence: composition attested to 1714 at Vienna; the work is untitled by Leibniz and published posthumously
stops.campa: The answer runs to ninety numbered paragraphs and carries no title. Substance is finally simple, indivisible, without windows, a single point of view on the whole universe, and there are infinitely many of them, each mirroring all the others without ever touching one. He writes it in French, in Vienna, near the end of his life. Others print it after his death and call it the Monadologie. Gilles Deleuze will spend an entire book on it in 1988, reading the monad as a fold rather than a point.
stops.quote: There are two kinds of truths: those of reasoning and those of fact. The truths of reasoning are necessary and their opposite is impossible; the truths of fact are contingent and their opposites are possible.
stops.quote_source: Leibniz, La Monadologie (1714), proposition 33, quoted on Wikiquote
suggested_refs: La Monadologie (1714), first published posthumously
Gilles Deleuze, Le Pli: Leibniz et le baroque (Minuit, 1988)

stops.name: Hanover, the Elector becomes a king
stops.date_confidence: Queen Anne dies 1 August 1714; the Hanoverian departure follows within weeks
stops.campa: Queen Anne dies and Georg Ludwig of Hanover, whose family's claim Leibniz's own genealogical labor helped to document, becomes King George the First of Great Britain. The whole court packs for London. Leibniz, returning from Vienna, is told he may not follow until the history of the House of Brunswick is finished, and it is not finished. The Electress Sophia, who would have been queen, had died in the Herrenhausen garden on the eighth of June, two months short of a throne.
suggested_refs: The Hanoverian succession of 1714
Sophia of Hanover, died 8 June 1714 at Herrenhausen

stops.name: Bad Pyrmont, the Tsar at the spa
stops.date_confidence: attested to June 1716 at the spa town; the meeting is not documented as taking place inside the Schloss, whose coordinates are used here
stops.campa: He travels to the spa at Bad Pyrmont and meets Tsar Peter the Great, who made him a privy counsellor of justice in 1711 and has been taking his advice on Russian administration since about 1708. It is one of the last journeys he makes. The academy of sciences he urges on the Tsar opens at St Petersburg in 1725. For several days at the spa the two of them talk about colleges and mines, about magnetic declination, about collecting the languages of Siberia before they are gone.
suggested_refs: Schloss Pyrmont and the spa at Bad Pyrmont
Leibniz's memoranda to Peter the Great on a Russian academy of sciences

stops.name: Hanover, the house on the Schmiedestraße
stops.date_confidence: attested to the day
stops.campa: He dies on the fourteenth of November in the house on the Schmiedestraße he has occupied since September 1698, of gout and a remedy he prescribed himself. He is seventy. The court is in London. The history of the House of Brunswick stands unfinished somewhere in the eleventh century, and the correspondence, some fifteen thousand letters, is boxed and carried to the ducal library, where editors are still working through it. Estimates of how many people he wrote to run from six hundred to over eleven hundred and are not reconciled.
stops.quote: I have enjoyed little leisure, being so weighted down of late with occupations of a totally different nature.
stops.quote_source: Leibniz, letter to Abbé Antonio Conti, 9 April 1716, quoted in the Wikipedia article 'Leibniz-Newton calculus controversy'
suggested_refs: The Leibnizhaus, Schmiedestraße 10, destroyed 1943, facade rebuilt 1981-1983 at the Holzmarkt
The Leibniz Nachlass at the Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz Bibliothek, Hanover

stops.name: Hanover, the Neustädter Kirche
stops.date_confidence: burial follows the death of 14 November 1716 by an interval the reachable sources do not fix; coordinates reconcile three conflicting values in the research pool to the German Wikipedia position for the church
stops.campa: He is buried in the Neustädter Hof- und Stadtkirche St. Johannis. His secretary Eckhart attends. No courtier comes, and no representative of the Royal Society that elected him, or of the Berlin Academy that he founded and presided over. The grave lies unmarked for more than fifty years and is eventually covered by a plain plaque reading OSSA LEIBNITII, the bones of Leibniz. The church itself is wrecked by bombing in 1943 and rebuilt in the decade after the war.
stops.quote: He was buried more like a robber than what he really was, the ornament of his century.
stops.quote_source: Eyewitness account of Leibniz's funeral, quoted in the MacTutor biography of Leibniz; the witness is unnamed in the source
suggested_refs: The Neustädter Hof- und Stadtkirche St. Johannis, Hanover, and the OSSA LEIBNITII plaque
sources: MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz'
German Wikipedia, 'Neustädter Hof- und Stadtkirche St. Johannis'

stops.name: Paris, Fontenelle speaks for the Academy
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the date of the Academy's public session for the éloge was not fixed in the sources reached, so the day defaults to 01-01
stops.campa: The Académie Royale des Sciences of France, which refused him membership in 1675 and admitted him only around 1700, hears its secretary Bernard le Bovier de Fontenelle deliver the éloge that neither Hanover nor London nor Berlin has offered. Fontenelle has the whole of it in front of him: the boy in his father's library, the machine, the calculus, the arithmetic of one and zero, forty years of court service, the history nobody will ever finish. The praise is spoken in the one city that never gave him a post.
suggested_refs: Fontenelle's Éloge de M. Leibnitz, Académie Royale des Sciences, 1717
